Revelation 1.summary: Revelation opens by calling itself “the revelation of Jesus Christ,” given by God to show his servants what must soon take place. John writes to seven churches in the Roman province of Asia, greeting them in the name of the eternal God, the seven spirits before his throne, and Jesus Christ, described as the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth. John says he was on the island of Patmos ‘on account of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus’ when, on the Lord’s Day, he heard a loud voice and turned to see seven golden lampstands and, among them, one ‘like a son of man.’ The figure’s appearance is overwhelming: white hair, eyes like flame, feet like burnished bronze, a voice like rushing waters, seven stars in his right hand, and a sharp two-edged sword coming from his mouth. John falls as though dead, but Christ lays his right hand on him, tells him not to fear, identifies himself as the First and the Last who died and is alive forevermore, and commands John to write what he has seen. The chapter closes by explaining that the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches and the lampstands are the seven churches themselves.
Revelation 1.whereWeAre:
John says he is on Patmos ‘on account of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus.’ The text does not say who sent him there or whether he was exiled or came to preach.

Rome used certain islands as places of banishment for some offenders. Many readers therefore understand John’s presence on Patmos as exile, though the chapter does not state this directly.

Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.30.3) places the vision near the end of Domitian’s reign, and later writers such as Victorinus and Eusebius say John was exiled to Patmos under Domitian. Whether Domitian carried out a broad, empire-wide persecution of Christians is debated by modern historians, and the evidence for it is limited.

John describes shared tribulation with his readers, which shows the churches were already under some pressure. The kind and extent of that pressure varied by city (see chapters 2–3).

Christians in Asia lived where emperor worship (the imperial cult) was well established. The extent of any formal requirement on Christians is uncertain. The vision of Christ as ruler of kings, holder of death’s keys, and the one who stands among his churches speaks directly to a small minority group living under a powerful empire and facing social or legal pressure. The chapter assures them of Christ’s authority before any specific warnings are given.

keyFigures.name: John
keyFigures.role: He receives the vision, is commanded to write it down, and sends it to seven churches. He is the human witness through whom the message reaches the churches. His self-description as a fellow sufferer shows he shares his readers’ situation.

keyFigures.name: Jesus Christ
keyFigures.role: He is the source of the revelation, the one who is coming, and the speaker who comforts and commissions John. The chapter presents him as sharing divine titles (First and Last, the living one) and holding the keys of Death and Hades, which sets the tone for the entire book.

keyFigures.name: God the Father (‘the Alpha and the Omega’)
keyFigures.role: He gives the revelation to Christ and speaks in 1:8. His eternity and power ground the confidence of the whole book: the one who began history also finishes it.

keyFigures.name: The seven spirits before the throne
keyFigures.role: They are named as a source of grace and peace. Their exact identity is disputed (see interpretive notes), but their inclusion in the greeting shows they share in giving blessing.

keyFigures.name: The seven churches
keyFigures.role: They are the first recipients of the book and are represented by the lampstands. Christ’s presence among the lampstands shows his ongoing care and oversight of his people.

keyFigures.name: The angels of the seven churches
keyFigures.role: They are mentioned in Christ’s explanation of the vision. That the stars are in Christ’s hand pictures his protection and authority over each church.

keyFigures.name: Roman imperial authority
keyFigures.role: It is not a character in the chapter. It is part of the background to John’s mention of tribulation and of Christ’s kingship. Claiming Christ as ruler of earthly kings would have carried weight in a world where Rome claimed supreme rule.

keyThemes.theme: The sovereignty of the risen Christ
keyThemes.explanation:
Christ is described as ruler of the kings of the earth, the First and the Last, the living one, and the holder of the keys of Death and Hades.

Readers are invited to take courage from the fact that the one who speaks to them has already faced death and now holds authority over it.

The glorified Christ stands in the midst of the lampstands and holds the stars in his right hand.

The chapter presents Christ as near his people, not distant from them.

keyThemes.theme: Blessing for hearing and keeping the message
keyThemes.explanation:
The chapter begins with a blessing on the one who reads aloud and those who hear and keep what is written, because ‘the time is near.’

The text emphasizes responsive obedience alongside understanding.

keyThemes.theme: A people redeemed to be a kingdom and priests
keyThemes.explanation:
Christ loves his people, freed them by his blood, and made them a kingdom and priests to God.

Their identity rests on what Christ has done, not on their standing in the eyes of the empire.

John describes himself as a partner in ‘tribulation and the kingdom and the patient endurance that are in Jesus.’

Faithfulness under pressure is presented as part of belonging to Christ’s kingdom.

Revelation 2.summary: In chapter 2 Christ dictates the first four of seven letters to churches in Asia. Each letter has a similar pattern: a description of Christ drawn from the vision in chapter 1, a statement of what he knows about the church (“I know…”), commendation and/or concern, a call to respond, and a promise to ‘the one who conquers.’ Ephesus is praised for hard work, endurance, and testing false apostles, but has abandoned its first love. Smyrna is poor and facing slander and coming imprisonment, yet Christ calls it rich and urges faithfulness even to death. Pergamum lives ‘where Satan’s throne is,’ has held fast to Christ’s name even when Antipas was killed, but tolerates people who hold the teaching of Balaam and the Nicolaitans. Thyatira is commended for love, faith, service, and growing works, but is rebuked for tolerating a woman symbolically called “Jezebel,” who misleads Christ’s servants into sexual immorality and eating food sacrificed to idols. Each letter includes the line, ‘He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.’
Revelation 2.whereWeAre:
Ephesus was a leading port and provincial center. Its temple of Artemis was one of the best-known sanctuaries of the ancient world. Acts 19 records a riot there centered on Artemis worship and the silversmith trade.

Ephesus also had temples connected with the imperial cult, including one for the emperor Domitian built around AD 89–90, according to archaeological and inscriptional evidence.

Smyrna was a prosperous port with a long record of loyalty to Rome. Tacitus (Annals 4.15, 4.55-56) records Smyrna’s claim to have been the first city to build a temple to Rome (usually dated to 195 BC) and its success in AD 26 in winning the right to build a temple to the emperor Tiberius.

Smyrna had a Jewish community. The text says some there who claim to be Jews are a “synagogue of Satan.” The kind of conflict is not described in detail, so the specifics are not known.

Pergamum had an early temple to Augustus and Roma (about 29 BC), a famous library, a large altar to Zeus on its acropolis, and a major healing sanctuary dedicated to Asclepius.

Thyatira was a commercial city with many trade guilds, known from inscriptions. Acts 16:14 mentions Lydia, ‘a seller of purple goods’ from Thyatira. Guild membership often involved shared meals and ceremonies connected to patron gods.

Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, was martyred in a year traditionally dated to AD 155–156 (some scholars argue for a later date), long after John’s time. He is not mentioned in the chapter, but his later story shows the pressure Christians in Smyrna faced. Trade, civic life, and public religion were intertwined in these cities. A believer who refused to join guild feasts, civic ceremonies, or emperor worship could face economic and social costs. This is the background for the warnings about food sacrificed to idols and for the tension between compromise and faithfulness in Pergamum and Thyatira.

keyFigures.name: Jesus Christ
keyFigures.role: He examines, commends, corrects, and promises. Each description is matched to the needs of the church addressed, showing his knowledge and authority.

keyFigures.name: The church in Ephesus
keyFigures.role: It is commended for endurance and doctrinal vigilance, and warned for losing its first love. Shows that correct belief and hard work are not enough if love for Christ cools.

keyFigures.name: The church in Smyrna
keyFigures.role: It faces poverty, slander, and coming imprisonment, and receives no rebuke. Presents suffering believers as spiritually rich and promises them life beyond death.

keyFigures.name: The church in Pergamum
keyFigures.role: It is faithful under pressure but tolerates false teaching. Illustrates the danger of internal compromise as well as external pressure.

keyFigures.name: The church in Thyatira
keyFigures.role: It grows in works but tolerates a false teacher. Shows that active service does not excuse tolerating false teaching.

keyFigures.name: Antipas
keyFigures.role: He is mentioned as an example of faithfulness unto death. Nothing else is stated in Scripture about him. Later traditions about how he died exist but are not part of the text and cannot be verified, so the details are unknown.

keyFigures.name: The Nicolaitans
keyFigures.role: Ephesus is praised for hating their works; Pergamum is rebuked for having those who hold their teaching. They show that false teaching was a real concern in several congregations.

keyFigures.name: Balaam
keyFigures.role: Referenced only as a pattern: his “teaching” led people to eat food offered to idols and commit sexual immorality (2:14). He is not a character in the chapter. The reference ties Pergamum’s problem to an old pattern of compromise.

keyFigures.name: “Jezebel” of Thyatira
keyFigures.role: She teaches and leads Christ’s servants into sexual immorality and eating food offered to idols. She is given time to repent but refuses. She shows the problem of tolerating a leader who encourages compromise.

keyFigures.name: ‘The one who conquers’
keyFigures.role: Each letter ends with a promise to this person. Victory in Revelation is defined as faithfulness to Christ, even to death (compare 2:10).

keyThemes.theme: Christ’s intimate knowledge of his churches
keyThemes.explanation:
Each letter begins with “I know,” and Christ says he searches minds and hearts.

The letters invite honest self-examination in the knowledge that Christ sees accurately.

Ephesus defended truth but lost its first love, while Thyatira had love and service but tolerated false teaching.

The text calls for both faithfulness to teaching and warmth toward Christ.

Smyrna faces poverty, slander, and coming imprisonment, and Christ calls it to be faithful “unto death” (2:10); Pergamum is commended for holding fast even when Antipas was killed (2:13).

Hardship is not evidence that Christ has abandoned his people.

keyThemes.theme: Danger of compromise with idolatry and immorality
keyThemes.explanation:
Pergamum and Thyatira are warned about the teaching of Balaam, the Nicolaitans, and “Jezebel,” which are connected with eating food sacrificed to idols and sexual immorality.

The text treats tolerance of leaders who lead believers into sin as a serious failure.

Each letter includes a distinct promise to the one who conquers: the tree of life, protection from the second death, hidden manna and a new name, authority over the nations and the morning star.

Faithfulness is linked to a future shared with Christ.

explainedReferences.explanation: Revelation directly repeats the psalm's imagery of ruling with a rod of iron and breaking pottery.

Revelation 3.summary: Chapter 3 completes the seven letters. Sardis has a reputation for being alive, but Christ says it is dead. He calls it to wake up, strengthen what remains, remember what it received, and repent. A few in Sardis have not soiled their garments and will walk with him in white. Philadelphia has little power but has kept Christ’s word and not denied his name. Christ sets before it an open door that no one can shut, promises that those who oppose it will be made to acknowledge his love for it, and promises to keep it from the coming hour of trial. Laodicea, rich and self-satisfied, is told it is lukewarm, ‘wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked.’ Christ advises it to buy from him gold refined by fire, white garments, and salve for its eyes, and says he disciplines those he loves. He ends with the well-known invitation: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock.” Each letter ends with a promise to the one who conquers and the call to hear what the Spirit says to the churches.
Revelation 3.whereWeAre:
Sardis was once the capital of the kingdom of Lydia and associated with the king Croesus. Its acropolis was thought to be unassailable but was captured by surprise attack, according to ancient historians, by Cyrus of Persia (about 546 BC, according to Herodotus) and later by Antiochus III (214 BC, according to Polybius). The warning to ‘wake up’ and the thief image fit a city remembered for such lapses of watchfulness, though the text does not say this connection is intended.

A major earthquake in AD 17 devastated Sardis and Philadelphia, among other cities of the region. Tacitus (Annals 2.47) records that the emperor Tiberius gave aid to Sardis.

Philadelphia was founded in the 2nd century BC by the kings of Pergamum and named for Attalus II Philadelphus (‘brother-lover’). The geographer Strabo (Geography 12.8.18; 13.4.10) notes that the region was subject to frequent earthquakes and that people in Philadelphia often left the city because of the shaking.

Laodicea was a wealthy trading city on a major road. Tacitus (Annals 14.27) reports that after an earthquake around AD 60–61 it rebuilt itself without imperial assistance. Cicero’s letters from the first century BC also show it as a financial center.

Laodicea was known in antiquity for its textile industry, and ancient sources connect the region with medical training and eye treatments. The details of the latter are less certain.

Laodicea relied on water brought by aqueduct. Hierapolis, a few miles north, had hot mineral springs, and Colossae, to the east, had cold water. Archaeologists have found mineral deposits in Laodicea’s water pipes.

Paul’s letter to the Colossians (4:13-16) mentions a church at Laodicea and a letter ‘from Laodicea.’ The church there existed before Revelation was written. Many interpreters see local references in the letters: Sardis’s history of unexpected conquest in the ‘thief’ warning, Philadelphia’s earthquake history in the promise of a stable ‘pillar,’ and Laodicea’s wealth, textile trade, medical reputation, and water supply in the language of gold, white garments, eye salve, and lukewarm water. These connections are widely proposed but cannot be proven; the letters can be understood without them.

keyFigures.name: Jesus Christ
keyFigures.role: He evaluates and addresses each church. His descriptions are matched to each church’s need: living power for dead Sardis, authority for weak Philadelphia, truthful witness for self-deceived Laodicea.

keyFigures.name: The church in Sardis
keyFigures.role: It is warned that it is spiritually dead and must wake up. Reputation and reality can differ.

keyFigures.name: The few in Sardis
keyFigures.role: They are promised they will walk with Christ in white. Faithfulness can exist in a small remnant inside a failing church.

keyFigures.name: The church in Philadelphia
keyFigures.role: It receives no rebuke and is promised an open door and protection. Strength in the eyes of God is not measured by size or power.

keyFigures.name: Opponents in Philadelphia (“the synagogue of Satan”)
keyFigures.role: They oppose the church but will be made to acknowledge Christ’s love for it. Shows vindication of the faithful.

keyFigures.name: The church in Laodicea
keyFigures.role: It receives a severe rebuke with no commendation, yet also a warm invitation. Self-sufficiency can block awareness of one’s need for Christ.

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: He is not a character but the source of the image of royal authority. Christ’s control of the key shows his authority to open and shut.

keyThemes.explanation:
Sardis seems alive but is dead. Laodicea thinks it is rich but is poor. Philadelphia seems weak but is faithful.

The chapter encourages honest self-examination.

Sardis is told to “wake up” and strengthen what remains. Laodicea is told to be zealous and repent.

Repentance is presented as an available response, with clear urgency.

Philadelphia has little power yet has kept Christ’s word. It is told to hold fast so that no one will seize its crown.

Endurance matters most when circumstances are difficult.

Christ says, ‘Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline,’ and then stands at the door and knocks.

Rebuke and love are not opposed in this passage.

The promises include white garments, a name in the book of life, a pillar in the temple, and a seat on Christ’s throne.

The promises are tied to faithful perseverance and anticipate the final chapters of the book.

Revelation 4.summary: After the letters to the churches, John sees a door standing open in heaven and hears the voice from chapter 1 invite him: ‘Come up here, and I will show you what must take place after this.’ Immediately he is “in the Spirit” and sees a throne with someone seated on it, whose appearance is like jasper and carnelian, surrounded by a rainbow that looks like an emerald. Around the throne are twenty-four other thrones with twenty-four elders in white clothes and golden crowns. Lightning, rumblings, and thunder come from the throne, seven torches of fire burn before it, and before it is something like a sea of glass, like crystal. Around the throne are four living creatures covered with eyes, described as like a lion, an ox, a man, and a flying eagle. Day and night they never stop saying, ‘Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come.’ Whenever they give glory, the twenty-four elders fall down, cast their crowns before the throne, and worship God as Creator, saying he is worthy to receive glory and honor and power because he created all things.
Revelation 4.whereWeAre:
Roman rulers in the first century were publicly honored with titles, temples, and ceremonies in the cities of Asia. Some emperors were called ‘lord’ and ‘savior.’ Suetonius (Domitian 13) reports that Domitian was addressed as ‘lord and god’ in official documents, though modern historians debate how widely this was applied.

The Old Testament includes throne-room visions: Isaiah 6, Ezekiel 1, and Daniel 7. Revelation 4 draws on all three in language and imagery.

Jewish and early Christian readers familiar with these visions would have recognized the combination of a throne, fiery elements, winged living creatures, and a crystal-like expanse (compare Ezekiel 1:22, 26-28). For readers living in a world where imperial honors were prominent, the vision offers a different picture of ultimate power and worship. The wording of the praise in 4:11, ‘Worthy are you, our Lord and God,’ is often compared with imperial acclamations, though the text does not explicitly say it is a response to the emperor cult.

keyFigures.name: John
keyFigures.role: He observes and describes the scene. As a witness, he gives readers access to what he saw.

keyFigures.name: The one seated on the throne (God)
keyFigures.role: He is the center of the scene and the object of all worship. His rule over all things, including creation, makes him the foundation of hope for the rest of the book.

keyFigures.name: The twenty-four elders
keyFigures.role: They fall down in worship and cast their crowns before the throne. They show that all rule and honor belong to God and are surrendered to him.

keyFigures.name: The four living creatures
keyFigures.role: They lead continuous praise of God’s holiness. They embody ceaseless worship and awareness.

keyFigures.name: The seven spirits of God
keyFigures.role: They are part of the throne-room scene. They emphasize the presence and power of God’s Spirit (a common reading), though the identity is debated.

keyThemes.explanation:
A throne dominates the scene, and the word ‘throne’ is used repeatedly in the chapter. God is not described as threatened or opposed here.

Readers are invited to see earthly events in light of God’s rule.

The four living creatures proclaim ‘Holy, holy, holy,’ echoing (Isaiah 6:3), and the scene includes lightning, thunder, and awe.

Worship is the fitting response to who God is.

The elders praise God because he created all things and by his will they existed and were created.

Creation is the basis of worship and of confidence in God’s purposes.

The elders cast their crowns before the throne.

The passage presents worship as ceasing to rely on one’s own status.

God is called the one ‘who was and is and is to come’ and the one who lives ‘forever and ever.’

Confidence in God’s unchanging nature supports perseverance.

Revelation 5.summary: John continues to watch the scene around God’s throne. He sees a scroll in the right hand of the one seated there, written on both sides and sealed with seven seals. A mighty angel calls out, ‘Who is worthy to open the scroll and break its seals?’ but no one in heaven, on earth, or under the earth is able to open it or even look into it. John weeps greatly. One of the elders tells him not to weep because ‘the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered’ and can open the scroll. But when John looks, he sees not a lion but a Lamb standing, ‘as though it had been slain,’ with seven horns and seven eyes. The Lamb takes the scroll from the right hand of the one on the throne. When he has taken it, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fall down before the Lamb with harps and golden bowls of incense, and they sing a new song declaring that the Lamb is worthy because he was slain and by his blood ransomed people for God from every tribe, language, people, and nation. Countless angels join in, and finally every creature in heaven, on earth, under the earth, and in the sea praises both the one on the throne and the Lamb.
Revelation 5.whereWeAre:
Many Jews in the first century expected a Davidic Messiah who would defeat Israel’s enemies. Genesis 49:9-10 and Isaiah 11:1-10 were among the passages used for such hopes. Revelation 5 draws on these texts.

Christians in Asia were part of a society where public honors for the emperor and local gods were common. The Lamb’s worship alongside God would contrast with this.

The Lamb recalls the Passover lamb (Exodus 12) and the suffering servant who was ‘led like a lamb to the slaughter’ (Isaiah 53:7). Elsewhere in the New Testament, Jesus is called the Lamb of God (John 1:29) and Paul calls Christ ‘our Passover lamb’ (1 Corinthians 5:7). The announcement of a Lion and the vision of a slain Lamb together show readers that Jesus fulfills messianic hopes in an unexpected way. For churches facing pressure, it affirms that suffering does not mean defeat.

keyFigures.name: The one seated on the throne (God)
keyFigures.role: He holds the sealed scroll in his right hand and gives it to the Lamb. He is the source of the scroll and of the plan it represents.

keyFigures.name: The Lamb (Jesus Christ)
keyFigures.role: He is found worthy to take the scroll and open its seals. He fulfills the Old Testament hopes of a victorious Davidic king (the Lion, the Root) but wins by being slain.

keyFigures.name: The mighty angel
keyFigures.role: He asks who is worthy to open the scroll. His question frames the problem the Lamb resolves.

keyFigures.name: John
keyFigures.role: He weeps when no one can open the scroll and is comforted by an elder. His reaction and relief express the weight of the question.

keyFigures.name: One of the elders
keyFigures.role: He tells John to stop weeping and announces the Lion of Judah. He acts as an interpreter within the vision.

keyFigures.name: The four living creatures and twenty-four elders
keyFigures.role: They fall before the Lamb and sing the new song. They direct worship to the Lamb as well as to God.

keyFigures.name: Myriads of angels
keyFigures.role: They proclaim sevenfold praise to the Lamb. They represent the greatness of the praise.

keyFigures.name: The saints (those ransomed from every tribe, language, people, and nation)
keyFigures.role: They are the beneficiaries of his work. The universal scope of the redeemed is emphasized.

keyFigures.name: Judah and David
keyFigures.role: They are referenced in titles only. The titles root the Lamb’s identity in Israel’s promises.

keyThemes.explanation:
No one in heaven, on earth, or under the earth can open the scroll except the Lamb.

The text directs attention and trust to Christ as the one worthy to bring history to its goal.

John hears about a Lion but sees a slain Lamb. The Lamb has ‘conquered’ (5:5) by being slain (5:6, 5:9).

Christ’s victory is defined by his sacrificial death, which shapes how his followers understand victory (compare 12:11).

keyThemes.theme: Redemption of people from every nation
keyThemes.explanation:
The Lamb ransomed people ‘from every tribe and language and people and nation.’

The scope of the Lamb’s work is universal.

keyThemes.theme: Kingdom and priesthood of the redeemed
keyThemes.explanation:
The Lamb has made his people ‘a kingdom and priests to our God.’

Redeemed people share in Christ’s reign and serve God.

keyThemes.theme: Worship of God and the Lamb together
keyThemes.explanation:
Praise goes both to the one on the throne and to the Lamb, and all creation joins.

Worship is the proper response to Christ’s work.

Revelation 6.summary: The Lamb begins to open the seven seals of the scroll. When he opens the first four, a living creature calls out ‘Come,’ and four horsemen appear in turn. The first rides a white horse and carries a bow, and is given a crown and goes out conquering. The second rides a red horse and is permitted to take peace from the earth so that people slay one another, and is given a great sword. The third rides a black horse and holds a pair of scales. A voice announces that a quart of wheat and three quarts of barley will each cost a denarius and that the oil and wine are not to be harmed. The fourth rides a pale horse whose rider is named Death, followed by Hades, who are given authority over a fourth of the earth to kill with sword, famine, plague, and wild beasts. At the fifth seal, John sees under the altar the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God and their testimony. They cry out, ‘How long, O Lord, holy and true?’ and are given white robes and told to rest a little longer until the number of their fellow servants who are to be killed is complete. The sixth seal brings a great earthquake, the sun turning black, the moon like blood, stars falling, the sky rolled up, and every mountain and island removed. People from every rank hide and cry out for mountains to fall on them to hide them from ‘the wrath of the Lamb’ and ask, ‘Who can stand?’
Revelation 6.whereWeAre:
The Roman Empire expanded by military conquest and maintained order by force. Tacitus (Agricola 30) puts a speech in the mouth of a Caledonian (Scottish) chief criticizing Roman conquest: ‘They make a desolation and call it peace.’ It shows how some conquered peoples viewed Roman ‘peace,’ though it is the historian’s written version of the speech.

The empire experienced wars and civil conflict in the first century, including the civil wars of AD 68–69. Rome’s eastern frontier faced Parthia, whose mounted archers were famous. Some interpreters see the white horse with a bow as an allusion to Parthian forces, but this is a proposal.

Famines are recorded in the first century in various regions; Acts 11:28 mentions a famine under Claudius. Suetonius (Domitian 7.2) reports that Domitian, after a grain shortage, issued an edict forbidding new vineyards in Italy and ordering vineyards in the provinces to be cut back (it was later not enforced, according to Suetonius, Domitian 14.2). Some scholars connect this to the oil-and-wine detail of 6:6. This is a proposed link and not certain, and many date Revelation differently.

Christians were killed for their faith at times in the first century. Nero blamed Christians for the fire of Rome in AD 64 (Tacitus, Annals 15.44). The text of Revelation 6 does not specify where or when the martyrs were killed.

Earthquakes were common in the region and caused serious damage, as in AD 17 and around AD 60 (see chapter 3). Cosmic-disturbance language like that in the sixth seal also appears in Old Testament prophecies of God’s judgment (Joel 2:10, 31; Isaiah 13:10; 34:4). The riders portray forces known to every reader in the ancient world: conquest, civil violence, scarcity, and death. For readers facing persecution, the fifth seal also acknowledges that some believers had already died for their faith, and the sixth speaks to the question of whether the powerful would escape accountability.

keyFigures.name: The Lamb
keyFigures.role: He opens each of the six seals. Because he opens the seals, the events are connected to his authority.

keyFigures.name: The four living creatures
keyFigures.role: Each of the first four calls ‘Come’ as the seals are opened. They are involved in the unfolding events from within the throne room.

keyFigures.name: The rider on the white horse
keyFigures.role: He goes out conquering. He introduces the series of riders.

keyFigures.name: The rider on the red horse
keyFigures.role: He takes peace from the earth so people slay one another. He represents violent conflict.

keyFigures.name: The rider on the black horse
keyFigures.role: He represents food shortage and high prices. The scales and grain prices depict famine.

keyFigures.name: Death and Hades
keyFigures.role: They are given authority over a fourth of the earth. Their authority is ‘given,’ implying limits, and Christ’s keys in 1:18 give context.

keyFigures.name: The souls under the altar
keyFigures.role: They cry out for justice and are told to wait. They show that martyrs are remembered and that justice is delayed but certain.

keyFigures.name: The kings, great ones, generals, rich, powerful, slaves, and free
keyFigures.role: They hide from God’s wrath and cry out to the mountains. Judgment reaches all classes, both high and low.

keyFigures.name: God (‘him who is seated on the throne’)
keyFigures.role: The people want to hide from his face. Together with ‘the wrath of the Lamb,’ it links the two in judgment.

keyThemes.explanation:
The riders and later events come as the Lamb opens each seal, and powers are ‘given.’

The text locates hard events within God’s oversight.

keyThemes.theme: The cost of human sin and violence
keyThemes.explanation:
Conquest, war, famine, and death are portrayed as destructive forces released on the earth.

The book does not minimize the severity of human suffering.

The martyrs ask when God will judge and avenge their blood, and are told to rest a little longer.

Believers may bring honest cries for justice to God while trusting his timing.

The martyrs are given white robes.

Faithful witness is valued even when it ends in death.

keyThemes.theme: The inescapable wrath of God and the Lamb
keyThemes.explanation:
People of every rank try to hide from the one on the throne and the Lamb.

The text treats the final judgment as serious and universal.

Revelation 7.summary: Chapter 7 pauses between the sixth and seventh seals and many readers see it as answering the question that ended chapter 6: ‘Who can stand?’ John sees four angels at the four corners of the earth holding back the four winds so that no wind blows on earth, sea, or trees. Another angel rises from the east with the seal of the living God and calls out to the four angels not to harm the earth until the servants of God have been sealed on their foreheads. John hears the number of those sealed: 144,000 from all the tribes of the sons of Israel, 12,000 from each of twelve named tribes. Then John sees a great multitude that no one could count, from every nation, tribe, people, and language, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, wearing white robes and holding palm branches. They cry out that salvation belongs to God and to the Lamb, and the angels, elders, and four living creatures fall on their faces in worship. One of the elders asks John who the people in white are and explains that they have come out of the great tribulation and have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb. Therefore they are before God’s throne and serve him day and night in his temple. They will never again hunger or thirst, the Lamb will shepherd them, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.
Revelation 7.whereWeAre:
In the Old Testament, Israel was organized as twelve tribes. After the Assyrian conquest of the northern kingdom (about 722 BC), the ten northern tribes were scattered. By the first century, the tribal identities were not clearly maintained, though some people still knew their tribe (for example, Paul was of Benjamin, Philippians 3:5; Anna of Asher, Luke 2:36).

The Christian communities in Asia included both Jewish and Gentile believers. The relationship between them, and between the church and Israel, was a major topic in the New Testament (for example, Romans 9–11; Galatians 3:28-29).

Christians in Asia were experiencing pressure of varying degrees (see chapters 2–3). For believers wondering whether they would survive trials and judgment, the chapter shows both protection (the seal) and a final destiny (the multitude before the throne). The language of Israel’s tribes helps convey that the church inherits and fulfills Israel’s promises, in the view of many interpreters, though others see a continuing role for ethnic Israel.

keyFigures.name: The four angels at the corners of the earth
keyFigures.role: They hold back the four winds. The delay shows that destructive forces operate only within God’s permission.

keyFigures.name: The angel with the seal of the living God
keyFigures.role: He directs the sealing of God’s servants. Sealing marks ownership and protection.

keyFigures.name: The 144,000
keyFigures.role: They are sealed on their foreheads before the harm to earth. They are known and secured by God.

keyFigures.name: The great multitude
keyFigures.role: They stand before the throne and the Lamb and sing of salvation. They show the global scope of salvation and the final state of God’s people.

keyFigures.name: One of the elders
keyFigures.role: He questions John and explains who the multitude are. He supplies the interpretation John does not already have.

keyFigures.name: John
keyFigures.role: He answers ‘Sir, you know,’ deferring to the elder. His response invites readers to receive the explanation.

keyFigures.name: The Lamb and God on the throne
keyFigures.role: Salvation is attributed to both; the Lamb shepherds the multitude and God shelters them. They are the source of salvation and care.

keyFigures.name: The twelve tribes of Israel
keyFigures.role: They are the groups from which 12,000 each are sealed. The tribal framework recalls God’s covenant people.

keyThemes.explanation:
The sealing of God’s servants takes place before harm is allowed to proceed.

The text assures readers that God knows and secures his own.

keyThemes.theme: Salvation belongs to God and the Lamb
keyThemes.explanation:
The multitude cries, ‘Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!’ and white robes are washed in the Lamb’s blood.

The chapter bases the believers’ standing on the Lamb’s sacrifice.

The multitude comes ‘from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages.’

The people of God are not limited to one group.

The multitude has ‘come out of the great tribulation.’

Faithfulness through hardship is honored.

God shelters them, they hunger and thirst no more, the Lamb shepherds them to springs of living water, and God wipes away every tear.

The passage offers hope for those who suffer.

Revelation 8.summary: When the Lamb opens the seventh seal, there is silence in heaven for about half an hour. Then John sees seven angels who stand before God and are given seven trumpets. Another angel with a golden censer stands at the altar and is given much incense to offer with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar before the throne. The smoke of the incense with the prayers rises before God. The angel then fills the censer with fire from the altar and throws it on the earth, and there are peals of thunder, rumblings, flashes of lightning, and an earthquake. The seven angels prepare to sound their trumpets. At the first trumpet, hail and fire mixed with blood are thrown on the earth, and a third of the earth, trees, and all green grass is burned up. At the second, something like a great burning mountain is thrown into the sea, and a third of the sea becomes blood, a third of the sea creatures die, and a third of the ships are destroyed. At the third, a great star called Wormwood falls on a third of the rivers and springs, and many die from the bitter water. At the fourth, a third of the sun, moon, and stars is struck so that a third of their light is darkened. John then sees and hears an eagle flying in midheaven crying out, ‘Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth, at the blasts of the other trumpets that the three angels are about to blow!’
Revelation 8.whereWeAre:
Trumpets (shofars and metal trumpets) were used in Israel to announce festivals, to sound alarms in war, and to signal God’s presence or judgment (Numbers 10:1-10; Joshua 6; Joel 2:1).

The Jerusalem temple was destroyed by Roman forces under Titus in AD 70, as recorded by the historian Josephus (Jewish War, Book 6). If Revelation was written after that date (the most common view), its readers would have understood the temple imagery as heavenly or symbolic rather than as a description of a standing temple service in Jerusalem.

Natural disasters, including earthquakes and volcanic eruptions, were known in the Mediterranean region. Pliny the Younger describes the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79 in his letters (6.16; 6.20). Whether this is relevant to Revelation 8 is uncertain.

Rome depended on sea trade, and ships were a major part of the economy. Chapter 18 later speaks of the loss of sea trade. The echoes of the Exodus plagues would have been clear to readers familiar with Scripture, making a link between God’s rescue of Israel from Egypt and his coming judgment. The incense-and-prayer scene draws on temple worship, assuring readers that their prayers matter in heaven.

keyFigures.name: The Lamb
keyFigures.role: He opens the seventh seal. He is not directly mentioned after 8:1, but the opening begins the trumpet sequence. The trumpets proceed from the seventh seal he opens.

keyFigures.name: The seven angels with trumpets
keyFigures.role: They sound the trumpets in turn. They carry out announced judgments.

keyFigures.name: The angel with the golden censer
keyFigures.role: He offers incense with the prayers of the saints and then throws fire from the altar to the earth. He links the prayers of God’s people with the judgments.

keyFigures.name: The saints
keyFigures.role: Their prayers are offered with the incense. Their prayers are received and connected to God’s action. This echoes 6:9-10.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: He receives the prayers and the sequence proceeds under his authority. He is the ultimate agent of the judgments.

keyFigures.name: Wormwood
keyFigures.role: It makes a third of the waters bitter. It is a symbol of bitterness and poison.

keyFigures.name: The eagle (or angel) in midheaven
keyFigures.role: It warns of the three remaining trumpets. It heightens the sense of increasing severity.

keyFigures.name: Those who dwell on the earth
keyFigures.role: They are the objects of the woes. It marks those who have chosen not to follow the Lamb.

keyThemes.theme: Prayers of the saints are heard
keyThemes.explanation:
The incense offered with the prayers of all the saints rises before God, and the fire from the altar is thrown to the earth.

The passage presents prayer as significant and not ignored.

keyThemes.theme: God’s judgment is measured and purposeful
keyThemes.explanation:
The trumpet plagues affect ‘a third’ of the earth, sea, waters, and heavenly lights.

Judgment in this chapter allows time for response.

Hail and fire (Exodus 9:23-25), water turned to blood (Exodus 7:20-21), and darkness (Exodus 10:21-23) recall the plagues on Egypt.

The imagery shows continuity in God’s dealings with injustice.

Earth, sea, rivers, and sky are struck.

The passage presents sin and judgment as having wide effects.

The eagle’s cry of three woes signals more severe events to come.

The text emphasizes the seriousness of what lies ahead.

Revelation 9.summary: At the fifth trumpet, John sees a star that has fallen from heaven to earth, who is given the key to the shaft of the bottomless pit. When the shaft is opened, smoke rises like the smoke of a great furnace and darkens the sun. Out of the smoke come locusts that are given power like that of scorpions, but they are told not to harm grass or trees, only people who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads. They are allowed to torment but not kill them for five months, and people will seek death but not find it. The locusts look like horses prepared for battle, with crowns like gold, human faces, hair like women’s hair, teeth like lions’ teeth, breastplates like iron, the sound of wings like many chariots, and tails like scorpions. Their king is the angel of the bottomless pit, named Abaddon in Hebrew and Apollyon in Greek. The first woe is past. At the sixth trumpet, a voice from the golden altar commands that the four angels bound at the great river Euphrates be released. They have been prepared for the hour, day, month, and year to kill a third of mankind. John hears the number of their mounted troops: twice ten thousand times ten thousand. The horses have heads like lions and breathe fire, smoke, and sulfur, and a third of mankind is killed by these three plagues. Yet the rest of mankind do not repent of the works of their hands, nor stop worshiping demons and idols, nor repent of their murders, sorceries, sexual immorality, or thefts.
Revelation 9.whereWeAre:
The plague of locusts in Egypt (Exodus 10:1-20) and the prophet Joel’s description of a locust-like invading army (Joel 1–2) provide the background for the fifth trumpet. Joel compares locusts to horses and war chariots (Joel 2:4-5).

Locust swarms were a known threat to farmland in the ancient Mediterranean and Near East and could devastate crops.

The Euphrates River formed the eastern frontier zone of Roman Syria and neighboring regions. Beyond it lay the Parthian Empire. The Parthians were famous for mounted archers, and at Carrhae in 53 BC they defeated a Roman army under Crassus, according to Plutarch and Cassius Dio.

In the Old Testament, invaders from the Euphrates region, such as Assyria and Babylon, are described as instruments of God’s judgment (Isaiah 8:7; Jeremiah 46:10).

The idolatry in 9:20 matches the widespread worship of images in the Greco-Roman world. Old Testament passages describe such idols as of gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood, and stone (compare Psalm 115:4-7; Daniel 5:4, 23).

The Roman Empire’s entire standing army in the first century is estimated by historians at a few hundred thousand soldiers, so the figure of 200 million is far beyond any human army of the time. For first-century readers, the locust and cavalry imagery echoed familiar biblical judgments, while the Euphrates evoked a feared frontier. The hardness of the survivors reflects the book’s ongoing concern with idolatry and pressure to compromise.

keyFigures.name: The fallen star
keyFigures.role: He opens the pit. He shows that the release of destructive forces is under granted authority.

keyFigures.name: The locusts
keyFigures.role: They torment people without God’s seal for five months. They are limited in both target and effect, and they contrast with those sealed in chapter 7.

keyFigures.name: Abaddon / Apollyon
keyFigures.role: He is king over the locusts. He is a figure of destruction; the text does not equate him with Satan, although some interpreters do.

keyFigures.name: The sixth angel and the voice from the golden altar
keyFigures.role: The voice commands the release of the four angels. The altar may recall the prayers of the saints (8:3-5).

keyFigures.name: The four angels bound at the Euphrates
keyFigures.role: They are released to kill a third of mankind. Their release at ‘the hour, the day, the month, and the year’ shows God’s control over timing.

keyFigures.name: The mounted army
keyFigures.role: They kill a third of humanity with fire, smoke, and sulfur. Their size conveys overwhelming force.

keyFigures.name: The rest of mankind
keyFigures.role: They persist in idolatry and sin. Their refusal to repent is the chapter’s concluding note.

keyFigures.name: Those who have the seal of God
keyFigures.role: The locusts are not allowed to harm them. They illustrate the protection described in chapter 7.

keyThemes.explanation:
The locusts are ‘given’ power, told not to harm certain things, and limited to five months. The sixth trumpet’s angels are released at a precise time.

The text emphasizes divine control even in the midst of terrifying scenes.

The locusts may harm only those who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads.

Those who belong to God are distinguished from others.

After the plagues, the rest of mankind do not repent.

The text portrays repentance as a matter of the heart, not merely of circumstances.

The failure to repent is described as continuing to worship demons and idols made of gold, silver, bronze, stone, and wood, and persisting in murder, sorcery, sexual immorality, and theft.

What a person worships is shown in how they live.

The abyss, the angel of the abyss, and bound angels indicate unseen spiritual realities.

The book portrays the conflict as larger than visible politics.

Revelation 10.summary: Between the sixth and seventh trumpets, John sees another mighty angel coming down from heaven. He is wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, a face like the sun, and legs like pillars of fire. In his hand is a little scroll, open. He plants his right foot on the sea and his left on the land and calls out in a loud voice like a lion’s roar. Seven thunders answer, and John is about to write what they said when a voice from heaven tells him to seal up what the seven thunders said and not write it down. The angel then raises his right hand to heaven and swears by the God who lives forever and ever, the Creator of heaven, earth, and sea, that there will be no more delay. In the days when the seventh angel is about to sound his trumpet, the mystery of God will be fulfilled, just as he announced to his servants the prophets. The voice from heaven then tells John to take the open scroll from the angel. The angel tells him to take it and eat it, saying it will be bitter in his stomach but sweet as honey in his mouth. John eats it, and it is as the angel said. He is then told, ‘You must again prophesy about many peoples and nations and languages and kings.’
Revelation 10.whereWeAre:
The Old Testament prophet Ezekiel was commissioned to eat a scroll with words of lamentation and woe, which tasted sweet (Ezekiel 2:8–3:3). Jeremiah also spoke of God’s words as a delight (Jeremiah 15:16).

In Daniel 12, an angel stands over the river, raises both hands to heaven, and swears by the one who lives forever concerning the time of the end, and Daniel is told to seal up the words (Daniel 12:4, 7). Unlike Daniel, John is later told not to seal up the words of this book (22:10), although the seven thunders are sealed.

The readers lived in a sea-trading region of the Roman world where the sea and land, together, would be understood as the whole world. The Roman Empire claimed dominion over land and sea (the Latin phrase terra marique ‘by land and sea’ was commonly used).

Many first-century Christians were awaiting the fulfillment of God’s promises while experiencing social and sometimes legal pressure. The oath that there will be no more delay speaks to people asking ‘How long?’ (6:10). The renewed commission to prophesy to kings and nations gives their witness a global purpose that stands over against Roman claims.

keyFigures.name: The mighty angel
keyFigures.role: He holds the little scroll, swears an oath, and gives the scroll to John. He signals that the final phase is near and passes the message to John.

keyFigures.name: The seven thunders
keyFigures.role: John is told not to write what they said. They show that not all that John saw or heard is recorded.

keyFigures.name: The voice from heaven
keyFigures.role: It tells John to seal up the thunders and later to take the scroll. It directs John’s role as a prophet.

keyFigures.name: God, the Creator
keyFigures.role: The angel swears by him. His authority as Creator guarantees the oath.

keyFigures.name: John
keyFigures.role: He is told not to write, to take and eat the scroll, and to prophesy again. He is renewed as a prophet to the nations.

keyFigures.name: The prophets
keyFigures.role: They are mentioned as those to whom the mystery was announced. They show continuity with the Old Testament message.

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel
keyFigures.role: He is not mentioned in Revelation 10, but the scene closely parallels his commission. The parallel presents John as a prophet in the same tradition.

keyThemes.explanation:
The angel swears that there will be no more delay and that the mystery of God will be fulfilled.

The text emphasizes God’s faithfulness to complete what he has announced.

keyThemes.theme: The prophetic task and the word of God
keyThemes.explanation:
John must take, eat, and then prophesy again.

The passage presents prophecy as requiring full reception of God’s word.

The scroll is sweet in the mouth and bitter in the stomach.

The text does not offer a simple, entirely pleasant message.

John is told not to write what the seven thunders said.

The text models humility about what is not revealed.

John must prophesy about many peoples, nations, languages, and kings.

The message concerns all humanity, not only one group.

Revelation 11.summary: John is given a measuring rod and told to measure the temple of God, the altar, and those who worship there, but to leave out the outer court, because it has been given over to the nations, who will trample the holy city for forty-two months. God will grant authority to his two witnesses, who will prophesy for 1,260 days, clothed in sackcloth. They are called the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth. If anyone tries to harm them, fire pours from their mouths and consumes their enemies. They have power to shut the sky so that no rain falls, to turn the waters into blood, and to strike the earth with plagues. When they have finished their testimony, the beast that comes up from the bottomless pit makes war on them, conquers them, and kills them. Their bodies lie in the street of the great city, which is symbolically called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified. People from the peoples, tribes, languages, and nations gaze at their bodies for three and a half days and refuse to bury them, and the inhabitants of the earth rejoice and exchange gifts. But after three and a half days, the breath of life from God enters them, and they stand on their feet. They are called up to heaven in a cloud, and a great earthquake strikes the city, killing seven thousand, and the rest give glory to the God of heaven. The second woe is past. The seventh angel then blows his trumpet, and loud voices in heaven announce that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of the Lord and of his Christ, and he will reign forever and ever. The twenty-four elders worship God, who has taken his great power and begun to reign, and God’s temple in heaven is opened, revealing the ark of his covenant, with flashes of lightning, rumblings, thunder, an earthquake, and heavy hail.
Revelation 11.whereWeAre:
Roman forces under Titus destroyed Jerusalem and its temple in AD 70, as recorded by Josephus (Jewish War, books 5–6). Jerusalem was then under Roman control, and the temple was not rebuilt.

After the destruction, the Roman government redirected the annual temple tax paid by Jews to the temple of Jupiter Capitolinus in Rome, according to Josephus (Jewish War 7.218) and Suetonius (Domitian 12), who also reports harsh enforcement of this tax under Domitian.

The Old Testament prophet Zechariah (ch. 4) saw a lampstand and two olive trees, which are interpreted there as ‘the two anointed ones who stand by the Lord of the whole earth’ (Zech 4:14). Elijah (1 Kings 17:1; 2 Kings 1:10-12) and Moses (Exodus 7–11) performed the miracles recalled in 11:5-6.

Daniel (7:25; 12:7) speaks of ‘a time, times, and half a time’ of oppression, and Daniel 8:13-14 and 9:27 refer to desecration of the temple. The desecration of the Jerusalem temple by Antiochus IV Epiphanes began in 167 BC and was reversed in 164 BC (1 Maccabees 1:54; 4:52), a period of roughly three years. Many interpreters see this episode as part of the background for Daniel’s time periods, and so indirectly for Revelation’s.

Christians in Asia were not under Jerusalem’s control, but Jerusalem’s fall affected Jews and Christians across the empire. The measuring of the temple, the trampling of the city, and the witnesses’ vindication would have spoken to believers who knew of Jerusalem’s fall and were themselves experiencing pressure. The picture of faithful witness leading to death and resurrection parallels Christ’s own pattern.

keyFigures.name: John
keyFigures.role: He is given a measuring rod and told to measure the temple. His measuring act represents protection or assessment.

keyFigures.name: The two witnesses
keyFigures.role: They prophesy 1,260 days, are killed, then raised and taken to heaven. They show faithful witness, vindicated after death.

keyFigures.name: The nations
keyFigures.role: The outer court is given to them, and they trample the holy city for forty-two months. They represent the force that opposes God’s people for a limited time.

keyFigures.name: The beast from the bottomless pit
keyFigures.role: It makes war on the witnesses and kills them. It represents the power opposing God’s witnesses.

keyFigures.name: Those who dwell on the earth and the peoples
keyFigures.role: They celebrate the witnesses’ deaths and exchange gifts. They show the world’s hostility to prophetic witness.

keyFigures.name: The survivors who give glory to God
keyFigures.role: They are terrified and give glory to the God of heaven. It shows a response to God’s vindication of the witnesses.

keyFigures.name: The seventh angel and the loud voices in heaven
keyFigures.role: They announce the kingdom. They mark the arrival of God’s reign.

keyFigures.name: The Lord and his Christ
keyFigures.role: The kingdom of the world becomes theirs, and he reigns forever. It declares the ultimate triumph of God’s rule.

keyFigures.name: The twenty-four elders
keyFigures.role: They worship God and give thanks. They interpret the meaning of the announcement.

keyFigures.name: Moses and Elijah, Zerubbabel and Joshua
keyFigures.role: They are not named in Revelation 11. They are background for the imagery. The echoes present the witnesses as continuing the work of the prophets.

keyThemes.theme: Faithful witness in a hostile world
keyThemes.explanation:
The two witnesses prophesy in sackcloth, and are opposed, overcome, and killed.

The text does not promise that faithful witness will be free from suffering.

After three and a half days, the witnesses are raised and taken to heaven.

Death is not the final word for faithful witnesses.

keyThemes.theme: God’s protection and limits on opposition
keyThemes.explanation:
The inner temple is measured while the outer court is trampled for forty-two months. The witnesses are protected until their testimony is finished.

The text portrays both suffering and a spiritual security that persists.

At the seventh trumpet, the kingdom of the world becomes the kingdom of the Lord and of his Christ.

History is moving toward God’s reign.

The elders speak of the time for the dead to be judged, for servants to be rewarded, and for destroyers of the earth to be destroyed.

The text presents God’s justice as including reward for faithful service.

Revelation 12.summary: John sees a great sign in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars on her head. She is pregnant and cries out in labor. Then another sign appears: a great red dragon with seven heads, ten horns, and seven diadems, whose tail sweeps down a third of the stars of heaven and throws them to the earth. The dragon stands before the woman so that he can devour her child as soon as it is born. She gives birth to a male child who is to rule all the nations with a rod of iron, and the child is caught up to God and to his throne. The woman flees into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, to be nourished for 1,260 days. War breaks out in heaven. Michael and his angels fight against the dragon and his angels, and the dragon is defeated and thrown down to the earth. He is identified as ‘that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world.’ A loud voice in heaven proclaims that salvation, power, and the kingdom of God and the authority of his Christ have come, because the accuser of the brothers has been thrown down. The brothers have conquered him ‘by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death.’ Woe comes to the earth and sea, since the devil has come down in great wrath, knowing his time is short. The dragon pursues the woman, who is given the two wings of the great eagle to fly to the wilderness, where she is nourished for a time, times, and half a time. The serpent pours water like a river from his mouth to sweep her away, but the earth swallows the river. Enraged, the dragon goes off to make war on the rest of her offspring, those who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus.
Revelation 12.whereWeAre:
Genesis 3:15 describes enmity between the serpent and the woman’s offspring, and Genesis 37:9-10 uses sun, moon, and eleven stars to represent Jacob’s family. Isaiah 66:7-9 and Micah 5:2-3 use childbirth imagery for Israel. Psalm 2:9 provides the ‘rod of iron.’

The Exodus story includes God carrying Israel ‘on eagles’ wings’ (Exodus 19:4) and feeding them in the wilderness (Exodus 16). Revelation 12 draws on this.

Herod the Great ordered the killing of infants in Bethlehem (Matthew 2:16). Some interpreters see an echo of the dragon’s attempt to destroy the child. Pharaoh’s attempt to kill Hebrew male infants (Exodus 1) is another parallel. The chapter does not refer explicitly to either.

Greek myth told of the goddess Leto, pursued by the python while pregnant with Apollo, who then killed the python. Ephesus (Artemis), Didyma and Claros (Apollo), and other Asian cities had prominent cults of Leto’s children. Some scholars suggest John’s readers would have noticed a contrast, but this is a proposal.

Roman coins and propaganda of the late first century portrayed emperors and their families in divine terms. Some coins of Domitian depict his deceased infant son as a child seated on a globe surrounded by stars. Some scholars have suggested a contrast with the true child, but this is a proposal and uncertain. For believers in Asia who were experiencing hostility from local authorities and neighbors, the chapter explains that the pressure they felt was part of a larger conflict, and that the decisive victory had already been won. The woman’s flight and nourishment gave comfort that they had not been abandoned.

keyFigures.name: The woman clothed with the sun
keyFigures.role: She gives birth to the child, is attacked by the dragon, and is protected in the wilderness. She represents the people from whom the Messiah comes and who are protected by God, in the view of most interpreters.

keyFigures.name: The male child (the Messiah)
keyFigures.role: He is born, threatened, and taken up to God. He shows that Satan’s attempts to destroy the Messiah fail.

keyFigures.name: The great red dragon (the devil / Satan)
keyFigures.role: He tries to devour the child, loses the war in heaven, is thrown down, and persecutes the woman and her offspring. He is the source of the opposition behind earthly persecution.

keyFigures.name: Michael and his angels
keyFigures.role: He and his angels fight and defeat the dragon. God’s forces overcome Satan’s forces.

keyFigures.name: The dragon’s angels
keyFigures.role: They lose the war and are thrown down to earth. They show that Satan has followers in the spiritual realm.

keyFigures.name: The brothers / those who conquered
keyFigures.role: They conquer by the blood of the Lamb, the word of their testimony, and not loving their lives even unto death. They show how victory is won.

keyFigures.name: The rest of her offspring
keyFigures.role: The dragon makes war on them. They are the believers still on earth.

keyFigures.name: A loud voice in heaven
keyFigures.role: It proclaims the arrival of salvation and warns the earth. It interprets the war in heaven.

keyThemes.explanation:
The dragon, identified as Satan, is the source of persecution of the woman’s offspring.

The text interprets earthly opposition in light of a spiritual battle.

The child is caught up to God, the dragon is cast down, and the voice declares that salvation and the kingdom have come.

The text bases believers’ confidence on a victory already won.

They conquer ‘by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death.’

The text calls for faithfulness, even at great cost.

The woman has a place prepared by God, is given eagle’s wings, and is nourished for 1,260 days; the earth swallows the dragon’s flood.

God provides for his people in the wilderness.

The devil is filled with great wrath ‘because he knows that his time is short.’

The text encourages endurance because opposition will end.

Revelation 13.summary: John sees a beast rising out of the sea with ten horns and seven heads, ten diadems on its horns and blasphemous names on its heads. It resembles a leopard, with feet like a bear’s and a mouth like a lion’s. The dragon (from chapter 12) gives it his power, his throne, and great authority. One of its heads seems to have a mortal wound, but the wound is healed, and the whole earth marvels and follows the beast. People worship the dragon and the beast, asking, ‘Who is like the beast, and who can fight against it?’ The beast is allowed to speak proud and blasphemous words and to exercise authority for forty-two months. It blasphemes God and his dwelling, makes war on the saints and conquers them, and receives authority over every tribe, people, language, and nation. All who dwell on the earth worship it, except those whose names have been written in the Lamb’s book of life. John then sees a second beast rising out of the earth, with two horns like a lamb but speaking like a dragon. It exercises the first beast’s authority, makes the earth worship the first beast, performs great signs (even making fire come down from heaven), and deceives those who dwell on earth. It orders them to make an image of the first beast, gives breath to the image so that it speaks, and has those who refuse to worship the image put to death. It also forces everyone, small and great, rich and poor, free and slave, to receive a mark on the right hand or forehead, so that no one can buy or sell unless he has the mark, which is the name of the beast or the number of its name. John adds: ‘This calls for wisdom. Let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and his number is 666.’
Revelation 13.whereWeAre:
Cities in Asia built temples to emperors. The temple of Augustus and Roma at Pergamum was dedicated about 29 BC. Smyrna was granted a temple to Tiberius in AD 26 (Tacitus, Annals 4.55-56). Ephesus had a temple of the Sebastoi (the emperors) dedicated in the time of Domitian, according to inscriptions.

Roman coins carried the emperor’s image and titles, some of which claimed divine status. Inscriptions in Asia honored Augustus in divine terms; the Priene calendar inscription (about 9 BC) calls him a savior and speaks of his birth as ‘good news.’

Nero, emperor from AD 54 to 68, blamed Christians for the fire of Rome in AD 64 and executed many (Tacitus, Annals 15.44). He died by suicide in AD 68. Rumors circulated that he had not really died or would return, recorded by Tacitus (Histories 2.8) and Suetonius (Nero 57). Several impostors claimed to be Nero. Some scholars see this ‘Nero legend’ behind the healed head wound; this is a proposal.

The practice of assigning numbers to names (isopsephy or gematria) was common in the Greek- and Hebrew-speaking world. A graffito from Pompeii reads, ‘I love her whose number is 545.’

Domitian (reigned AD 81–96) reportedly encouraged use of the title ‘lord and god’ according to Suetonius (Domitian 13). Whether this applied widely is debated.

Trade guilds and civic associations in Asian cities often held feasts and sacrifices honoring gods and emperors, so participation in business could involve religious participation. Scholars suggest this may be behind the buying and selling restriction, but the text does not specify.

In about AD 112, Pliny the Younger, governor of Bithynia (north of Asia), wrote to Emperor Trajan (Letter 10.96) that he tested accused Christians by having them offer incense and wine to the emperor’s image and curse Christ. This comes some years after Revelation and from a nearby province, so it is only contextual. For believers in Asia, the imperial cult, civic life, and trade were closely linked with public expressions of loyalty to Rome. The chapter portrays the demand for such loyalty as the demand to worship the dragon’s agent. Whether or not formal persecution was widespread when Revelation was written, local pressure, social exclusion, and occasional executions are described in the book (2:13).

keyFigures.name: The dragon (Satan)
keyFigures.role: He empowers the beast. The beast’s authority is derived from the dragon, not from God.

keyFigures.name: The beast from the sea
keyFigures.role: It rules, blasphemes, makes war on the saints, and receives worship. It represents a political power that demands what belongs to God. It is described as imitating the Lamb (slain, then alive).

keyFigures.name: The beast from the earth (later called the false prophet)
keyFigures.role: It promotes worship of the first beast, performs signs, makes the image, and enforces the mark. It stands for religious deception that supports political power.

keyFigures.name: The saints
keyFigures.role: They are targeted by the beast. They show the cost of faithfulness; the text calls for their endurance.

keyFigures.name: Those who dwell on the earth
keyFigures.role: They worship the beast and receive the mark. They are contrasted with the saints.

keyFigures.name: The Lamb
keyFigures.role: He owns the book of life. Belonging to him is set against worshiping the beast.

keyFigures.name: Roman emperors (including Nero)
keyFigures.role: They are part of the historical background, not characters in the text. Many scholars think the imperial cult, with its titles and worship of emperors, forms the background for the beast’s demand for worship.

keyThemes.explanation:
The beast has a mortal wound that is healed, receives authority, and is worshiped, echoing the Lamb who was slain and lives. The second beast looks like a lamb but speaks like a dragon.

The text warns that power and religion can appear impressive while opposing God.

The whole earth worships the dragon and the beast, and an image is made that must be worshiped.

The text treats allegiance as a matter of worship, not merely politics.

keyThemes.theme: Endurance and faithfulness of the saints
keyThemes.explanation:
The text calls for ‘the endurance and faith of the saints’ in the face of captivity and the sword.

Believers are encouraged to be faithful without presuming protection from suffering.

The beast is ‘given’ authority and a mouth, and rules ‘for forty-two months.’ The text repeats that authority was ‘given’ to it.

The text locates evil within boundaries even when it appears dominant.

No one can buy or sell without the mark.

The text recognizes that conviction may cost livelihood.

Revelation 14.summary: After the dark scenes of chapter 13, John sees the Lamb standing on Mount Zion with 144,000 who have his name and his Father’s name written on their foreheads. A sound from heaven like many waters and thunder, and like harpists playing, accompanies a new song before the throne that only the 144,000 can learn. They are described as redeemed from the earth, as those who have not defiled themselves with women (for they are ‘virgins’), who follow the Lamb wherever he goes, who were redeemed as firstfruits for God and the Lamb, and in whose mouth no lie was found. Three angels then fly in midheaven. The first has an eternal gospel to proclaim to every nation, tribe, language, and people: ‘Fear God and give him glory, because the hour of his judgment has come, and worship him who made heaven and earth.’ The second announces, ‘Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great.’ The third warns that anyone who worships the beast and its image and receives its mark will drink the wine of God’s wrath and be tormented with fire and sulfur. A call for endurance follows, and a voice from heaven says, ‘Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on.’ John then sees one like a son of man seated on a white cloud with a golden crown and a sharp sickle. An angel calls for him to reap, because the harvest of the earth is ripe, and the earth is reaped. Another angel comes out of the temple with a sharp sickle, and another from the altar tells him to gather the clusters of the vine of the earth, because its grapes are ripe. He throws them into the great winepress of the wrath of God, which is trodden outside the city, and blood flows from the winepress as high as horses’ bridles for 1,600 stadia.
Revelation 14.whereWeAre:
Mount Zion in the Old Testament is Jerusalem’s hill, the site of David’s city and, in prophetic hope, the place of God’s rule (Psalm 2:6; Joel 3:16-17; Isaiah 24:23). Jerusalem had been destroyed by Rome in AD 70.

‘Babylon’ was the capital of the empire that destroyed Jerusalem and the temple in 586 BC. After AD 70, some Jewish writings (for example, 2 Baruch and 4 Ezra) and early Christian writings (probably 1 Peter 5:13) used ‘Babylon’ as a code name for Rome. In Revelation, chapter 17 describes Babylon in ways that scholars most often connect with Rome.

The Old Testament prophets used harvest and winepress imagery for God’s judgment: Joel 3:13, Isaiah 63:1-6, and Jeremiah 51:33 (for Babylon).

Believers in Asia faced economic and social pressure to take part in civic and imperial religion, as discussed in chapter 13. Chapter 14 responds to the question raised by chapter 13: what of those who refuse the beast? They are with the Lamb, and their deaths are blessed. The announcement of Babylon’s fall would have encouraged those under Roman pressure, and the harvest assures them that judgment is coming.

keyFigures.name: The Lamb
keyFigures.role: He is with the 144,000 and they follow him. He contrasts with the beast: his people bear his name and follow him.

keyFigures.name: The 144,000
keyFigures.role: They sing a new song and follow the Lamb. They are the faithful who contrast with those who bear the beast’s mark.

keyFigures.name: The first angel
keyFigures.role: He calls all people to fear and worship God. He shows that a final call precedes judgment.

keyFigures.name: The second angel
keyFigures.role: He declares that Babylon has fallen. It introduces Babylon, whose fall is described in chapters 17–18.

keyFigures.name: The third angel
keyFigures.role: He pronounces judgment on worshipers of the beast. He gives a severe warning against receiving the mark.

keyFigures.name: Babylon the great
keyFigures.role: She is announced as fallen. Her fall is a central event of judgment.

keyFigures.name: The beast and its worshipers
keyFigures.role: Those who worship the beast face God’s wrath. Their fate contrasts with the dead who die in the Lord.

keyFigures.name: The one like a son of man
keyFigures.role: He reaps the harvest of the earth. He is the agent of the harvest.

keyFigures.name: The harvest angels
keyFigures.role: They call for the reaping and harvest the grapes. They carry out the final judgment.

keyFigures.name: The voice from heaven
keyFigures.role: It pronounces the blessing on the dead in the Lord. It brings comfort to the faithful.

keyThemes.theme: The Lamb and his faithful people
keyThemes.explanation:
The 144,000 have the names of the Lamb and the Father on their foreheads and follow the Lamb wherever he goes.

The text portrays faithful devotion to Christ as the opposite of allegiance to the beast.

keyThemes.theme: A call to all nations to worship the Creator
keyThemes.explanation:
The first angel proclaims an eternal gospel to every nation, tribe, language, and people.

The text emphasizes that God’s offer reaches all peoples.

keyThemes.theme: The fall of Babylon and judgment on the beast’s followers
keyThemes.explanation:
The second and third angels announce Babylon’s fall and God’s wrath on those who worship the beast.

The text presents judgment as real and serious.

keyThemes.theme: Endurance and rest for the faithful
keyThemes.explanation:
The call for endurance is followed by a blessing on those who die in the Lord, who rest from their labors, as their deeds follow them.

The text encourages perseverance, with assurance of rest and reward.

The harvest and the winepress are images of the end of history and of God’s wrath.

History moves to an end under God’s authority.

Revelation 15.summary: John sees another great and marvelous sign in heaven: seven angels with seven plagues, which are the last, because with them the wrath of God is finished. He sees what looks like a sea of glass mixed with fire, and standing beside it are those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name. They hold harps given by God and sing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb. Their song praises the Lord God Almighty for his great and amazing deeds, calls him just and true in his ways and King of the nations, asks who will not fear and glorify his name, declares that he alone is holy, and says that all nations will come and worship him because his righteous acts have been revealed. After this, the temple, the tent of witness, is opened in heaven, and the seven angels with the seven plagues come out, dressed in pure bright linen with golden sashes. One of the four living creatures gives the seven angels seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God, who lives forever and ever. The temple is filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his power, and no one can enter it until the seven plagues of the seven angels are finished.
Revelation 15.whereWeAre:
In the Exodus, Israel crossed the Red Sea and sang a song of victory led by Moses (Exodus 15:1-18). The plagues on Egypt preceded it (Exodus 7–12). Revelation 15–16 echoes this pattern.

The ‘tent of witness’ is another name for the tabernacle (Numbers 9:15; 17:7-8; Acts 7:44), which Israel carried in the wilderness. When the tabernacle was completed, the cloud and the glory of the Lord filled it, and Moses could not enter (Exodus 40:34-35). Similarly, the glory filled Solomon’s temple (1 Kings 8:10-11).

Christians in Asia faced pressure to worship the emperor, and some had been killed for refusing (see chapters 2 and 13). For readers facing pressure, the picture of conquerors singing the song of Moses presents their refusal to worship the beast as a participation in God’s deliverance, like Israel’s deliverance from Pharaoh. The Exodus background suggests that a ruler who defied God would face his judgment.

keyFigures.name: The seven angels with the seven last plagues
keyFigures.role: They are given the bowls of God’s wrath. They carry out the final series of judgments.

keyFigures.name: Those who conquered the beast
keyFigures.role: They stand by the sea of glass and sing. They show the outcome for those who refused the beast.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: His song is named as one of the songs sung. It links the deliverance of the faithful to Israel’s Exodus deliverance.

keyFigures.name: The Lamb
keyFigures.role: His song is sung alongside Moses’s. It shows that the new deliverance comes through him.

keyFigures.name: The Lord God Almighty, King of the nations
keyFigures.role: He is praised as just, true, holy, and worthy of the worship of all nations. His wrath is in the bowls. He is the one who judges.

keyFigures.name: One of the four living creatures
keyFigures.role: He gives the seven angels the golden bowls. It connects the plagues to the throne room.

keyFigures.name: The beast
keyFigures.role: Mentioned as the one the singers conquered. It marks the contrast between the singers and the beast’s followers.

keyThemes.explanation:
The song declares God’s ways ‘just and true’ and that he alone is holy.

The text invites readers to trust God’s justice even when judgment is severe.

Those who conquered the beast sing with harps from God.

The faithful are shown celebrating even before the final judgment is completed.

The sea, the song of Moses, and the plagues recall Israel’s deliverance from Egypt.

God’s earlier acts are presented as the pattern for his final ones.

The song says all nations will come and worship God.

The text expresses hope in the universal recognition of God.

keyThemes.theme: God’s presence and holiness in judgment
keyThemes.explanation:
The temple is filled with smoke and no one can enter until the plagues are finished.

The text portrays God as holy and approachable only on his terms.

Revelation 16.summary: A loud voice from the temple tells the seven angels to go and pour out the seven bowls of the wrath of God on the earth. The first angel pours his bowl on the earth, and harmful and painful sores break out on those who have the mark of the beast and worship its image.
