The second pours his on the sea, and it becomes like the blood of a dead man, and every living thing in the sea dies. The third pours his on the rivers and springs, and they become blood. The angel of the waters says God is just in these judgments because those people shed the blood of saints and prophets, and a voice from the altar agrees. The fourth bowl is poured on the sun, which scorches people with fire, yet they curse God and do not repent. The fifth is poured on the throne of the beast, and its kingdom is plunged into darkness; people gnaw their tongues in anguish and curse God but do not repent. The sixth is poured on the great river Euphrates, and its water is dried up to prepare the way for the kings from the east. Three unclean spirits like frogs come from the mouths of the dragon, the beast, and the false prophet, and they go out to the kings of the whole world to gather them for battle on the great day of God the Almighty. Christ interrupts: ‘Behold, I am coming like a thief! Blessed is the one who stays awake, keeping his garments on.’ The kings gather at a place called in Hebrew Armageddon. The seventh bowl is poured into the air, and a loud voice from the throne says, ‘It is done!’ There is lightning, thunder, and a massive earthquake like none before. The great city splits into three parts, the cities of the nations fall, and God remembers Babylon the great and gives her the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath. Every island flees, mountains disappear, and huge hailstones, each about the weight of a talent (often rendered ‘about a hundred pounds’), fall on people, who curse God for the plague.
Revelation 16.whereWeAre:
Several bowls echo the plagues on Egypt: sores (Exodus 9:8-12), water turned to blood (Exodus 7:17-21), darkness (Exodus 10:21-23), frogs (Exodus 8:1-15), and hail (Exodus 9:22-26).

The Euphrates marked the eastern edge of the Roman Empire in Syria. Beyond it was Parthia, the empire Rome could not fully conquer. The Roman people feared Parthian invasion. After Nero’s death in AD 68, pretenders claiming to be Nero appeared (Tacitus, Histories 1.2; 2.8-9), and Suetonius (Nero 57) says a later pretender, some twenty years after Nero’s death, had Parthian backing.

Cyrus of Persia took Babylon in 539 BC, according to ancient accounts, by diverting the Euphrates and entering along the riverbed (Herodotus 1.191; compare Isaiah 44:27–45:1; Jeremiah 50:38; 51:36). Some interpreters see an allusion to this in the drying of the Euphrates.

Megiddo overlooks the plain of Jezreel and was the site of battles recorded in the Old Testament, including Barak’s battle against Sisera (Judges 5:19) and Josiah’s death in battle against Pharaoh Necho (2 Kings 23:29).

Earthquakes were well known in Asia (see chapter 3), and hail is described in the Old Testament as a weapon of God (Joshua 10:11; Exodus 9). The plague imagery tells readers that God, who humbled Pharaoh, will deal with the empire that persecutes his people. The Euphrates and Megiddo imagery draw on geography and history familiar to readers to describe a final confrontation between the nations and God.

keyFigures.name: The seven angels with the bowls
keyFigures.role: They pour out the bowls in turn. They carry out the judgments.

keyFigures.name: A loud voice from the temple (God)
keyFigures.role: It commands the angels to pour out the bowls. It shows that judgments come at God’s command.

keyFigures.name: Those with the mark of the beast
keyFigures.role: They receive sores and later curse God. They are the objects of judgment and an example of unrepentance.

keyFigures.name: The angel of the waters
keyFigures.role: He declares God’s judgment just. He supplies the reason for the third bowl.

keyFigures.name: The altar
keyFigures.role: It affirms that God’s judgments are true and just. It links the judgments to the cry of the martyrs.

keyFigures.name: The dragon, the beast, and the false prophet
keyFigures.role: Unclean spirits come from their mouths to gather the kings. They are the sources of deception.

keyFigures.name: The three unclean spirits like frogs
keyFigures.role: They gather the kings of the whole world for battle. They represent deception that leads to confrontation.

keyFigures.name: The kings of the whole world and the kings from the east
keyFigures.role: They are gathered for the battle on the day of God. They show the nations in opposition to God.

keyFigures.name: Christ (the speaker of ‘I am coming like a thief’)
keyFigures.role: He gives a warning and a blessing. He calls readers to watchfulness.

keyFigures.name: Babylon the great
keyFigures.role: She receives the cup of God’s wrath. It anticipates chapters 17–18.

keyThemes.explanation:
The angel of the waters and the altar declare God ‘just’ and his judgments ‘true and just.’

The passage presents divine judgment as an expression of righteousness.

People curse God and do not repent after the fourth, fifth, and seventh bowls.

The text pictures repentance as a matter of the heart, not merely circumstances.

keyThemes.theme: Deception and the gathering of nations
keyThemes.explanation:
Demonic spirits perform signs and gather the kings for battle.

The text warns about signs and persuasion that lead away from God.

Christ says he comes like a thief and blesses the one who stays awake.

Readers are called to stay alert and keep their garments.

keyThemes.theme: The end of Babylon and the completion of judgment
keyThemes.explanation:
‘It is done!’ marks completion, and Babylon is remembered for judgment.

The text emphasizes the finality of God’s judgment.

Revelation 17.summary: One of the seven angels with the bowls invites John to see the judgment of the great prostitute who is seated on many waters, with whom the kings of the earth have committed sexual immorality, and with the wine of whose immorality the dwellers on earth have become drunk. The angel carries John in the Spirit into a wilderness, where he sees a woman sitting on a scarlet beast that is full of blasphemous names and has seven heads and ten horns. The woman is dressed in purple and scarlet and adorned with gold, jewels, and pearls. She holds a golden cup full of abominations and the impurities of her immorality. On her forehead is written a name of mystery: ‘Babylon the great, mother of prostitutes and of earth’s abominations.’ She is drunk with the blood of the saints and the martyrs of Jesus. John is greatly astonished, and the angel offers to explain the mystery of the woman and the beast. The beast ‘was, and is not, and is about to rise from the bottomless pit and go to destruction.’ The seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman is seated, and they are also seven kings, five of whom have fallen, one is, and the other has not yet come, and when he does come he must remain only a little while. The beast is an eighth that belongs to the seven and goes to destruction. The ten horns are ten kings who have not yet received royal power but who receive authority for one hour together with the beast. They are of one mind and give their power to the beast. They will make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with him are called and chosen and faithful. The waters where the prostitute sits are peoples, multitudes, nations, and languages. The ten horns and the beast will hate the prostitute, make her desolate and naked, devour her flesh, and burn her with fire, because God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose. The angel concludes: ‘The woman that you saw is the great city that has dominion over the kings of the earth.’
Revelation 17.whereWeAre:
Rome was known in antiquity as the city on seven hills. The Roman poet Virgil (Georgics 2.534-535) wrote that Rome had surrounded itself with a wall for seven hills, and Martial (Epigrams 4.64) and other writers call it the city of seven hills. Roman coins of Vespasian depict the goddess Roma seated on seven hills.

In Asia, Roma was worshiped as a goddess. Smyrna’s temple to Roma is traditionally dated to 195 BC (Tacitus, Annals 4.56), and Pergamum shared a temple with Augustus and Roma from about 29 BC.

Rome dominated the Mediterranean world through military power and tribute, and its wealth came in part from the provinces. Roman authors such as Tacitus record complaints about exploitation, such as the speech attributed to Calgacus (Agricola 30).

Nero executed Christians in Rome after the fire of AD 64, as recorded by Tacitus (Annals 15.44), who also describes the cruelty of the spectacle. Roman sources do not give a complete record of persecution in Asia, but (Revelation 2:13) mentions the death of Antipas in Pergamum.

‘Babylon’ was used as a name for Rome in Jewish writings after AD 70 (2 Baruch; 4 Ezra; Sibylline Oracles 5) and probably in 1 Peter 5:13.

The Roman emperors from Augustus to Domitian include: Augustus (31 BC–AD 14), Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius, Nero (to AD 68), then Galba, Otho, Vitellius (AD 68–69), Vespasian (69–79), Titus (79–81), and Domitian (81–96). This list helps in considering the debate on the seven kings. For first readers, a woman seated on seven hills, dominant over kings and wealthy, drunk on the blood of Christians, would likely have evoked Rome and its imperial cult. The Old Testament prophets used prostitution as an image of cities and nations that sold themselves for wealth and power, and the image of Babylon as an oppressor of God’s people would have been familiar.

keyFigures.name: The angel with a bowl
keyFigures.role: He shows John the vision and explains it. He is John’s interpreter.

keyFigures.name: John
keyFigures.role: He is carried in the Spirit to the wilderness and is astonished. His astonishment leads to the angel’s explanation.

keyFigures.name: The great prostitute (Babylon the great)
keyFigures.role: She corrupts the nations, persecutes the saints, and is destroyed by the beast and its kings. She represents an imperial power that seduces and kills.

keyFigures.name: The scarlet beast
keyFigures.role: It carries the woman and later turns on her. It represents the power behind the city.

keyFigures.name: The seven kings
keyFigures.role: They are explained as the beast’s seven heads. They show the series of rulers.

keyFigures.name: The ten kings
keyFigures.role: They give their power to the beast, fight the Lamb, and destroy the prostitute. They show that the nations turn on the system that dominated them.

keyFigures.name: The kings of the earth and the dwellers on the earth
keyFigures.role: They commit immorality with her and are drunk with her wine. They are the objects of her influence.

keyFigures.name: The saints and martyrs of Jesus
keyFigures.role: Their blood is on the woman. They are the victims whose deaths will be avenged.

keyFigures.name: The Lamb and his followers
keyFigures.role: They conquer the kings. They are the victors.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: He is shown directing events, though not by name. Even the destruction of Babylon is under his purpose.

keyThemes.theme: The seduction and corruption of power
keyThemes.explanation:
The prostitute intoxicates the kings and peoples with her immorality, wealth, and splendor.

The text warns against being drawn in by wealth and power that oppose God.

She is drunk with the blood of the saints and the martyrs of Jesus.

The text recognizes that faithful witness may bring death.

The beast and ten kings hate the prostitute, desolate her, and burn her with fire.

The text shows evil destroying itself within God’s purposes.

The kings make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb conquers them as Lord of lords and King of kings.

Faithful followers share in his victory.

God puts it into the kings’ hearts to carry out his purpose ‘until the words of God are fulfilled.’

The text encourages trust in God’s control even over hostile powers.

Revelation 18.summary: Another angel with great authority comes down from heaven, and the earth is made bright with his glory. He cries out, ‘Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!’ She has become a dwelling place for demons and a haunt for every unclean spirit, because all nations have drunk of the wine of her immorality, the kings of the earth have committed immorality with her, and the merchants of the earth have grown rich from the power of her luxurious living. Another voice from heaven calls, ‘Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues.’ Her sins have piled up to heaven, and God has remembered her iniquities. She is to be repaid for her deeds, and since she boasts, ‘I sit as a queen, I am no widow, and mourning I shall never see,’ her plagues will come in a single day: death, mourning, and famine, and she will be burned with fire. The kings of the earth who committed immorality with her, the merchants, and the shipmasters and sailors each stand far off and mourn, lamenting that in a single hour her judgment has come. The merchants’ lament includes a long list of goods, from gold, silver, pearls, and purple cloth to cinnamon, wine, grain, horses, and chariots, and ends with ‘slaves, that is, human souls.’ Heaven, the saints, apostles, and prophets are told to rejoice over her, because God has given judgment for them against her. A mighty angel then picks up a stone like a great millstone and throws it into the sea, saying that Babylon will be thrown down with violence and will be found no more. No music, craftsmanship, sound of the mill, light of a lamp, or voice of bride and bridegroom will be heard in her again. The reasons are given: her merchants were the great ones of the earth, all nations were deceived by her sorcery, and in her was found the blood of prophets and saints and of all who have been slain on earth.
Revelation 18.whereWeAre:
Rome imported large quantities of grain, especially from Egypt and North Africa. Josephus (Jewish War 2.383-386), in a speech he attributes to Agrippa II, says that Africa supplied Rome with grain for eight months of the year and Egypt for four. Grain ships landed at Puteoli and Ostia.

Rome imported luxury goods from across and beyond the empire. Pliny the Elder (Natural History 12.84) complained that Roman spending on goods from India, the Seres (the silk-producing East), and Arabia drained about 100 million sesterces out of the empire each year. Many of the goods in Revelation 18:12-13 (pearls, silk, spices, incense, ivory, citron wood) were luxury imports.

Slavery was a basic part of the Roman economy. Slaves worked in households, fields, mines, and trades, and they were bought and sold as property. Estimates of the share of slaves in the population differ, and exact numbers are debated.

Asian cities such as Ephesus, Smyrna, and Miletus were major ports. Merchants and shipowners in Asia depended on Rome’s markets and stability.

Babylon fell to Cyrus of Persia in 539 BC. Prophecies of its destruction (Isaiah 13:19-22; Jeremiah 51:37-43) speak of it becoming a desolate place for wild creatures. Tyre, a great merchant city, was mourned in a similar way in Ezekiel 27, with merchants and sailors lamenting.

In AD 64 a fire destroyed much of Rome, according to Tacitus (Annals 15.38-44), lasting several days. Some interpreters see an echo of this fire in the burning of Babylon; others hold that the chapter depicts a different, final event. This is not stated in the text. The chapter would have appealed to believers who were both tempted by and pressured by the wealth and trade networks of Rome, and who could see its dependence on exploitation. It also echoes the pattern of prophetic lament over a great commercial city (Tyre) and a great oppressive power (Babylon).

keyFigures.name: The angel with great authority
keyFigures.role: He announces the fall of Babylon. His glory shows he speaks with God’s authority.

keyFigures.name: A voice from heaven
keyFigures.role: It warns and instructs God’s people and calls for retribution. It links the judgment to God’s concern for his people.

keyFigures.name: Babylon the great
keyFigures.role: She falls and is destroyed. Her fall is the focus of the chapter.

keyFigures.name: God’s people (‘my people’)
keyFigures.role: They are warned to come out. They are called to separate themselves.

keyFigures.name: The kings of the earth
keyFigures.role: They weep and mourn from far away. They show the political side of her influence.

keyFigures.name: The merchants of the earth
keyFigures.role: They weep because no one buys their cargo. They show the economic dimension of her influence.

keyFigures.name: Shipmasters, sailors, and seafarers
keyFigures.role: They lament from a distance. They represent the global trade network dependent on the city.

keyFigures.name: Saints, apostles, and prophets
keyFigures.role: They are called to rejoice. God’s judgment is on their behalf.

keyFigures.name: The mighty angel with the millstone
keyFigures.role: He throws the stone into the sea as a sign. The act pictures sudden, final destruction.

keyFigures.name: The Lord God
keyFigures.role: He is the judge. Judgment belongs to him, not to humans.

keyThemes.theme: The fall of proud and exploitative systems
keyThemes.explanation:
Babylon boasts that she sits as queen and will never see mourning, yet her ruin comes suddenly.

The text warns that pride and self-glorification lead to downfall.

God’s people are told to ‘come out of her.’

The text calls believers to examine their participation in systems that oppose God.

The cargo list ends with ‘slaves, that is, human souls.’

The text criticizes wealth built on the exploitation of people.

Babylon is judged for the blood of prophets, saints, and all who have been slain.

The text assures believers that God remembers and avenges the innocent.

‘In a single hour’ is repeated three times.

The text presents judgment as certain.

Revelation 19.summary: Immediately after Babylon’s fall, John hears what sounds like the roar of a great multitude in heaven shouting ‘Hallelujah! Salvation and glory and power belong to our God, for his judgments are true and just.’ They praise God for judging the great prostitute and avenging the blood of his servants. The twenty-four elders and four living creatures fall down and worship God, saying ‘Amen. Hallelujah!’ A voice from the throne then calls for all his servants to praise God, and a great multitude, sounding like many waters and mighty thunder, proclaims that the Lord God Almighty reigns and that the marriage of the Lamb has come. His Bride has made herself ready, clothed in fine linen, which is the righteous deeds of the saints. An angel tells John to write, ‘Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.’ John falls at the angel’s feet to worship him, but the angel stops him, saying, ‘I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers… Worship God.’ Heaven then opens, and John sees a white horse. Its rider is called Faithful and True, and he judges and makes war in righteousness. His eyes are like a flame of fire, on his head are many diadems, and he has a name written that no one knows but himself. He is clothed in a robe dipped in blood and is called The Word of God. The armies of heaven, in fine linen, white and pure, follow him on white horses. From his mouth comes a sharp sword with which to strike the nations, he will rule them with a rod of iron, and he will tread the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God. On his robe and thigh is written ‘King of kings and Lord of lords.’ An angel standing in the sun summons the birds to the great supper of God to eat the flesh of kings, commanders, and others. The beast and the kings of the earth with their armies gather to make war against the rider and his army. The beast is captured along with the false prophet, and both are thrown alive into the lake of fire. The rest are killed by the sword that comes from the rider’s mouth, and the birds gorge themselves on their flesh.
Revelation 19.whereWeAre:
‘Hallelujah’ is a Hebrew expression meaning ‘praise the Lord’ (hallelu-yah). It appears in the Psalms (for example, Psalms 104–106, 111–113, 115–117, 135, 146–150). This chapter contains the only occurrences of the word in the New Testament (19:1, 3, 4, 6).

Roman victory parades (triumphs) were major public events. The victorious general rode in a chariot, sometimes drawn by white horses, in a procession with soldiers and captives. Josephus (Jewish War 7.119-157) describes the triumph of Vespasian and Titus after the Jewish war, in AD 71.

The title ‘king of kings’ was used by rulers in the Near East, including Persian and Parthian rulers, as shown in inscriptions and coins. In the Greek East emperors were addressed as ‘lord’ (kyrios) and ‘savior’ (sōtēr); Augustus and Tiberius avoided the Latin dominus, though Suetonius reports that Domitian liked ‘dominus et deus.’ In the Old Testament, the title appears in Ezekiel 26:7 and Daniel 2:37 for Nebuchadnezzar, and Deuteronomy 10:17 calls God ‘God of gods and Lord of lords.’

Imperial propaganda in Asia described the emperor as a victorious ruler over the nations. The vision of Christ as the rider is understood by many scholars as a counter-claim, but the text does not explicitly say this.

Israel was called the bride of the Lord in the prophets (Isaiah 54:5-6; Jeremiah 2:2; Hosea 2:19-20), and the New Testament applies the image to Christ and the church (2 Corinthians 11:2; Ephesians 5:25-32). After the story of Rome-like Babylon’s fall, the chapter shows an alternative celebration: a wedding feast and a true king. For believers facing pressure to honor the emperor as lord, the vision of Christ as King of kings was a declaration of ultimate allegiance.

keyFigures.name: The great multitude in heaven
keyFigures.role: They shout ‘Hallelujah’ for the judgment of the prostitute and the reign of God. They give the heavenly perspective on events on earth.

keyFigures.name: The twenty-four elders and four living creatures
keyFigures.role: They fall down and say, ‘Amen. Hallelujah!’. They confirm the praise.

keyFigures.name: The Lord God Almighty
keyFigures.role: He is praised for true and just judgment. He is the one whose reign is celebrated.

keyFigures.name: The Lamb and his Bride
keyFigures.role: Their marriage is announced. The images show intimacy and celebration.

keyFigures.name: The great prostitute
keyFigures.role: She is referred to as already judged. Her fall is the reason for praise.

keyFigures.name: The angel who speaks to John
keyFigures.role: He pronounces the blessing on those invited to the supper and corrects John. He directs worship to God alone.

keyFigures.name: John
keyFigures.role: He falls at the angel’s feet. His mistake teaches that only God is to be worshiped.

keyFigures.name: The rider on the white horse (Faithful and True, the Word of God, King of kings and Lord of lords)
keyFigures.role: He judges and makes war, strikes the nations with the sword from his mouth, and defeats the beast. He is the victorious king and judge.

keyFigures.name: The armies of heaven
keyFigures.role: They follow the rider. They accompany Christ in his victory.

keyFigures.name: The angel standing in the sun
keyFigures.role: He summons the birds to the great supper of God. He summons the birds to feast on those about to be slain, anticipating the defeat.

keyFigures.name: The beast, the kings of the earth, and their armies
keyFigures.role: They gather to fight the rider and are defeated. They show the final opposition to Christ.

keyFigures.name: The false prophet
keyFigures.role: He is captured and thrown into the lake of fire with the beast. His fate completes the judgment of the beast’s allies.

keyThemes.theme: Praise for God’s true and just judgment
keyThemes.explanation:
The multitude praises God because his judgments are true and just.

The text encourages trust in God’s righteousness.

‘The Lord our God the Almighty reigns.’

The text places hope in God’s rule over all.

The marriage supper of the Lamb is announced, and his Bride is clothed in fine linen.

The text portrays the future as a celebration.

The angel refuses John’s worship and says, ‘Worship God.’

The passage directs all worship to God.

The rider is called Faithful and True, judges in righteousness, and defeats the beast and kings.

The text presents Christ as the final judge and king.

Revelation 20.summary: John sees an angel coming down from heaven with the key to the bottomless pit and a great chain. The angel seizes the dragon, ‘that ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan,’ binds him for a thousand years, throws him into the pit, and shuts and seals it over him so that he cannot deceive the nations until the thousand years are ended. After that he must be released for a little while. John then sees thrones, and seated on them are those given authority to judge. He also sees the souls of those who had been beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and for the word of God, and those who had not worshiped the beast or its image or received its mark. They came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years. The rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were ended. This is called ‘the first resurrection.’ Blessed and holy are those who share in it; the second death has no power over them, and they will be priests of God and of Christ and will reign with him for the thousand years. When the thousand years are over, Satan is released from his prison and goes out to deceive the nations at the four corners of the earth, ‘Gog and Magog,’ to gather them for battle, in number like the sand of the sea. They surround the camp of the saints and the beloved city, but fire comes down from heaven and consumes them, and the devil is thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur where the beast and the false prophet already are, to be tormented day and night forever and ever. John then sees a great white throne and the one seated on it, from whose presence earth and sky flee away. The dead, great and small, stand before the throne. Books are opened, and another book, the book of life, is opened. The dead are judged according to what they had done as recorded in the books. The sea gives up its dead, and Death and Hades give up the dead in them, and each is judged according to what he had done. Death and Hades are thrown into the lake of fire, which is the second death. Anyone whose name was not found written in the book of life is thrown into the lake of fire.
Revelation 20.whereWeAre:
Ezekiel 38–39 describes a final attack by Gog of Magog against restored Israel, and God’s destruction of the attackers by fire and other means. Revelation uses the names for the nations of the whole world.

Daniel 7:9-14, 22, 27 describes thrones set, books opened, and the saints receiving the kingdom, which is background for 20:4, 11-12.

Some Jewish writings from around the first century expect a temporary messianic kingdom followed by the final age, with differing durations. For example, 2 Esdras 7:28–29 (also called 4 Ezra) (Latin text; other versions give different numbers, such as 30 years), written about AD 100, describes a temporary messianic reign that ends with the Messiah’s death. The thousand-year figure in Revelation 20 is distinctive and also reflects (Psalm 90:4).

Christians were executed in Roman times, sometimes by beheading, which was a form of execution applied to Roman citizens. Revelation 2:13 mentions the death of Antipas in Pergamum. Whether any widespread beheadings of Christians occurred in Asia when Revelation was written is not documented.

Roman governors judged from a tribunal (bema) and decided people’s fates. Paul stood before such judgment seats (Acts 25:6-12). The great white throne gives a judgment scene in contrast to human courts.

Many in the ancient world feared death at sea without burial, which may be why the sea giving up its dead is mentioned. This is a scholarly suggestion and is not stated in the text. For believers who had lost friends to execution and feared the same for themselves, the chapter assures them that those killed for their witness will live and reign, that the dragon behind the persecution will be defeated, and that all injustice will be judged before a perfectly just throne.

keyFigures.name: The angel with the key and chain
keyFigures.role: He binds Satan and locks him in the pit. It shows that Satan’s restraint is under God’s authority.

keyFigures.name: The dragon (the devil and Satan)
keyFigures.role: He is bound, released, and finally thrown into the lake of fire. His defeat is the culmination of the conflict in the book.

keyFigures.name: Those seated on thrones
keyFigures.role: They sit on thrones. They show delegated authority. Their identity is not specified.

keyFigures.name: The martyrs and faithful (‘souls of those who had been beheaded’)
keyFigures.role: They come to life and reign with Christ for a thousand years. They are vindicated.

keyFigures.name: Christ
keyFigures.role: The faithful reign with him. His reign is shared.

keyFigures.name: The rest of the dead
keyFigures.role: They stand before the great white throne. They face judgment.

keyFigures.name: The nations (Gog and Magog)
keyFigures.role: They attack the camp of the saints and the beloved city. They show that rebellion remains even after the thousand years.

keyFigures.name: The saints and the beloved city
keyFigures.role: They are surrounded but protected by fire from heaven. They show God’s protection.

keyFigures.name: The beast and the false prophet
keyFigures.role: They are described as already in the lake of fire. Their fate is shared by the devil.

keyFigures.name: The one seated on the great white throne
keyFigures.role: He judges the dead. He is the final judge.

keyFigures.name: Death and Hades
keyFigures.role: They give up the dead and are thrown into the lake of fire. Their destruction marks the end of death.

keyFigures.name: Gog of Magog
keyFigures.role: They are named in Revelation 20:8 as symbols for the nations, not as individuals. The reference draws on Ezekiel’s picture of a final attack on God’s people.

keyThemes.theme: Satan’s limited power and final defeat
keyThemes.explanation:
Satan is bound, released for a time, and finally thrown into the lake of fire.

The text offers assurance that evil will not have the last word.

keyThemes.theme: Vindication and reign of the faithful
keyThemes.explanation:
Those who were killed for their testimony reign with Christ and are priests of God.

The text honors faithful witness and promises participation in Christ’s reign.

The dead are judged according to what they had done as recorded in the books.

The text treats judgment as certain and just.

Those whose names are in the book of life are spared the second death.

Belonging to God, not only deeds, is central to the passage.

Death and Hades are thrown into the lake of fire.

The text anticipates the removal of death as the final enemy.

Revelation 21.summary: John sees a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and first earth have passed away, and the sea is no more. He sees the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared like a bride adorned for her husband. A loud voice from the throne declares, ‘Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God. He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away.’ The one seated on the throne says, ‘Behold, I am making all things new,’ tells John to write because the words are trustworthy and true, and says ‘It is done! I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end.’ He promises water from the spring of life to the thirsty, and an inheritance for the one who conquers, and warns that the cowardly, faithless, detestable, murderers, sexually immoral, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars will have their portion in the lake of fire, the second death. One of the seven bowl angels then shows John ‘the Bride, the wife of the Lamb.’ John is carried to a great high mountain and sees the holy city Jerusalem coming down out of heaven, shining with the glory of God like a jasper, clear as crystal. It has a great high wall with twelve gates, with twelve angels at the gates and the names of the twelve tribes of Israel on them, three gates on each side. The wall has twelve foundations with the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb. The angel measures the city with a golden measuring rod. It is laid out as a square, its length, width, and height equal, twelve thousand stadia (about 1,400 miles), and its wall is 144 cubits thick (or high). The wall is jasper, the city pure gold like clear glass, and the foundations are adorned with twelve kinds of precious stones. The twelve gates are twelve pearls, and the street of the city is pure gold, transparent as glass. There is no temple in the city, for the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb are its temple. The city has no need of sun or moon, for the glory of God gives it light and its lamp is the Lamb. The nations will walk by its light, and the kings of the earth will bring their glory into it. Its gates will never be shut by day, and there will be no night. Nothing unclean will ever enter it, nor anyone who does what is detestable or false, but only those who are written in the Lamb’s book of life.
Revelation 21.whereWeAre:
Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22 speak of new heavens and a new earth. Isaiah 25:8 speaks of God wiping away tears. Ezekiel 40–48 describes a visionary temple and city measured by a man with a measuring rod, with gates named for the tribes of Israel (Ezekiel 48:30-35), and ends with the city’s name, ‘The Lord is there.’

Jerusalem and its temple were destroyed by the Romans in AD 70 (Josephus, Jewish War, books 5–6). If Revelation was written after this event, as most scholars think, the vision of the new Jerusalem and the absence of a temple (21:22) would speak to a world where the physical temple was gone.

Roman writers (Tibullus and Ovid, for example) called Rome the ‘eternal city,’ and Virgil (Aeneid 1.278-279) has Jupiter promise the Romans ‘empire without end.’ The new Jerusalem is the eternal city that God builds.

The Roman world had cities whose splendor was admired. The city of Rome had marble and gold in public buildings. Gates of ancient cities were normally closed at night for protection (Joshua 2:5; Nehemiah 7:3), so a city whose gates are never shut conveys perfect safety.

Believers in Asia lived in cities with pagan temples, and the absence of a temple in the new Jerusalem (21:22) stands in contrast to the many temples in their cities. After the fall of Babylon (chapters 17–18), the vision of the new Jerusalem offers the opposite city: not a prostitute but a bride, not exploitation but healing, and not the false eternity of Rome but the real one. It encouraged believers facing loss and pressure to look to the final home God was preparing.

keyFigures.name: John
keyFigures.role: He sees the new heaven, new earth, and new Jerusalem, and is told to write. He is the witness.

keyFigures.name: God (the one seated on the throne)
keyFigures.role: He dwells with his people, makes all things new, and says, ‘It is done! I am the Alpha and the Omega.’. This is one of the few places where God himself speaks in the book (compare 1:8).

keyFigures.name: The loud voice from the throne
keyFigures.role: It announces God’s dwelling with man. It interprets the vision.

keyFigures.name: The new Jerusalem (the Bride, the wife of the Lamb)
keyFigures.role: She descends from heaven. She represents God’s people and dwelling.

keyFigures.name: The Lamb
keyFigures.role: He is the husband of the Bride, a temple, and the lamp of the city. The city’s life centers on him.

keyFigures.name: One of the seven bowl angels
keyFigures.role: He shows John the Bride and measures the city. The parallel contrasts the two cities.

keyFigures.name: The twelve tribes of Israel
keyFigures.role: Their names are on the twelve gates. They link the city to Israel’s heritage.

keyFigures.name: The twelve apostles of the Lamb
keyFigures.role: Their names are on the twelve foundations. They link the city to the church founded on the apostles.

keyFigures.name: The conquerors
keyFigures.role: They inherit these things and are promised the status of God’s sons. They are the recipients of the promises in chapters 2–3.

keyFigures.name: The nations and the kings of the earth
keyFigures.role: They walk by the city’s light and bring their glory into it. They show the inclusion of the nations.

keyFigures.name: The excluded (cowardly, faithless, etc.)
keyFigures.role: They have their portion in the lake of fire. They show a continuing distinction.

keyThemes.explanation:
‘The dwelling place of God is with man.’

The text presents closeness to God as the heart of the future hope.

God will wipe away every tear; death, mourning, crying, and pain are no more.

The text offers comfort for those who suffer.

A new heaven and earth, and God declares, ‘I am making all things new.’

Hope is directed toward renewal.

The city has walls, gates, glory, and nothing unclean may enter.

The text presents purity and safety.

The thirsty are invited to the water of life, while the cowardly, faithless, and others are warned.

The text calls readers to respond.

Revelation 22.summary: The angel shows John the river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb through the middle of the city’s street. On either side of the river is the tree of life, bearing twelve kinds of fruit, yielding its fruit each month, and its leaves are for the healing of the nations. There will no longer be any curse. The throne of God and of the Lamb will be in the city, and his servants will worship him. They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads. There will be no more night, no need for lamp or sun, for the Lord God will be their light, and they will reign forever and ever. The angel says that these words are trustworthy and true, and that the Lord, the God of the spirits of the prophets, has sent his angel to show his servants what must soon take place. Christ says, ‘Behold, I am coming soon. Blessed is the one who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book.’ John falls to worship the angel, who again refuses and says, ‘Worship God.’ John is told not to seal up the words of the prophecy because the time is near. Christ says he is coming soon with his recompense for each, and calls himself the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end. Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life and may enter the city by the gates; outside are the dogs, sorcerers, sexually immoral, murderers, idolaters, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood. Jesus declares that he sent his angel to testify to the churches, and that he is the root and the descendant of David and the bright morning star. The Spirit and the Bride say, ‘Come,’ and let the one who hears say, ‘Come.’ Let the one who is thirsty come, and let the one who desires take the water of life without price. John warns that anyone who adds to or takes away from the words of this book will face consequences described in the book. The one who testifies to these things says, ‘Surely I am coming soon.’ John replies, ‘Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!’ The book ends with the grace of the Lord Jesus be with all.
Revelation 22.whereWeAre:
The book began like a letter with a greeting (1:4-5) and ends like a letter with a benediction (22:21), similar to those in Paul’s letters.

Genesis 2–3 describes the river and the tree of life in Eden, and the curse after the Fall. Ezekiel 47:1-12 describes a river from the temple with trees whose leaves are for healing. Revelation 22 draws on both.

‘Come, Lord Jesus’ (22:20) corresponds to the Aramaic prayer ‘Maranatha’ (1 Corinthians 16:22), which was used in early Christian worship, as the Didache (10:6) also shows.

Warnings against altering a text appear in Deuteronomy (4:2; 12:32) and in other ancient writings, for example the Letter of Aristeas (310–311), where a curse is pronounced on anyone who adds to, changes, or omits from the translation of the Law.

The titles ‘root of David’ and ‘bright morning star’ draw on messianic passages such as Isaiah 11:1, 10 and Numbers 24:17, and the morning star was promised to the one who conquers in 2:28.

The believers who first received this book faced pressures described in chapters 2–3 and 13, and at least some would hear the book read aloud in their gatherings (1:3). The ending gathers the book’s themes for its first hearers: a coming Lord, a final home, a call to worship God alone, and an open invitation. The warning about altering the words protects the message for congregations who heard it read aloud, and the final prayer expresses the longing of believers under pressure.

keyFigures.name: The angel
keyFigures.role: He shows John the river and refuses John’s worship. He is a ‘fellow servant’ with John and the prophets.

keyFigures.name: John
keyFigures.role: He falls to worship the angel and answers ‘Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!’. He gives the personal response of faith.

keyFigures.name: God and the Lamb
keyFigures.role: The river flows from their throne, and the servants worship them. They are the source of life and light.

keyFigures.name: The servants of God
keyFigures.role: They worship, see his face, bear his name, and reign. They enjoy fellowship with God.

keyFigures.name: Jesus (the speaker of ‘I am coming soon’)
keyFigures.role: He promises to return, repays each according to deeds, and invites all to come. The book’s final promise is in his voice, and it closes with John’s response and a benediction.

keyFigures.name: The Lord, the God of the spirits of the prophets
keyFigures.role: He is the source of the message. It connects Revelation to the line of prophets.

keyFigures.name: The Spirit and the Bride
keyFigures.role: They say ‘Come.’. They join in the invitation and in the prayer for Christ’s return.

keyFigures.name: The thirsty
keyFigures.role: They are invited to take it freely. The invitation is open.

keyFigures.name: Those who wash their robes
keyFigures.role: They are blessed and may enter the city and eat from the tree of life. They illustrate the blessing.

keyFigures.name: Those outside
keyFigures.role: They are outside the city. They show the serious boundary between those who enter and those who do not.

keyFigures.name: The churches
keyFigures.role: The testimony is for them. It returns to chapter 1.

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: He is not a character. The title ties Jesus to the messianic promises.

keyThemes.explanation:
The river and tree of life, and the absence of the curse, echo (Genesis 2–3) and Ezekiel 47.

The text portrays salvation as healing and restoring creation.

God’s servants worship him, see his face, and have his name on their foreheads.

The text emphasizes that the greatest blessing is God himself.

keyThemes.theme: Christ’s coming and the call to readiness
keyThemes.explanation:
Christ says three times that he is coming soon and blesses those who keep the words of the book.

The text calls readers to faithful living and expectation.

John is told again not to worship the angel.

Worship belongs only to God.

The Spirit and the Bride say ‘Come,’ and the thirsty may take the water of life without price.

The text invites anyone to respond.
